title: Sharpen a kitchen knife on a whetstone at 15 to 20 degrees, both sides, then lay it down edge away
instruction: Sharpen the knife on the whetstone, then put it back on the chopping block.
context: Sharpening a kitchen knife is a familiar household chore: a dull knife slips and needs more force, and many home cooks keep a whetstone for it, as do cooks and butchers who look after their own knives. The trained skill is the angle: the blade is held 15 to 20 degrees off the stone and swept across it edge first from heel to tip (pushed on one face, pulled toward the body on the other), each face worked until a burr runs the whole edge, then the faces alternated; then the knife is laid down flat with its edge away from the body. Held too flat, the stone grinds the face behind the bevel and never reaches the edge; held too steep, it grinds a more obtuse edge that cuts less keenly; sharpening one face only pushes the edge over into a wire instead of making it sharp. Sharpness is measured, not judged by eye: an edge tester reads the grams of force the edge needs to cut a standard test filament.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0; headings are measured from +x toward +y. Chopping block: an end-grain maple butcher block, 12 x 22 x 8 cm, fixed, its center at (16.4, 8.5), its long side at heading 105 degrees (turned 15 degrees from the y axis), its top at z 8. Knife: a 165 mm santoku (Japanese kitchen knife), 140 g, steel blade 16.5 cm long, 4.5 cm tall at the heel and 2 mm thick, its spine running straight for 7 cm and then curving down to the tip, its edge straight with a 6 mm rise over the last 3 cm to the tip, and a bright 6 mm ground bevel along the edge, an octagonal magnolia handle 9.5 cm long and 1.8 to 2.0 cm across with a dark horn ferrule; its balance point 2 cm in front of the bolster. It lies flat on the block, face A down, edge facing away from the robot (heading 15 degrees), the tip pointing left along the block, the bolster at (18.4, 0.8) and the front 3 cm of the handle on the block, the rest of the handle reaching past the block's right-hand edge toward (20.9, -8.4) so a hand can close round it. Whetstone: an orange 1000-grit combination stone, 18 x 6 x 2.5 cm, in a black rubber non-slip holder (21 x 8 x 1.5 cm with end clamps 3 cm tall) on a 6 cm wooden sharpening stand, all fixed, centered at (39.4, -5.5), its long side at heading -15 degrees (pointing away from the robot and slightly right), the stone's top at z 10. The left arm is not needed; both arms start at their home pose. For a real trial the edge starts dull in the same way every time: with the stone soaked, hold the knife upright, edge straight down on the stone, and draw the whole edge once along the stone's length, heel to tip, pressing about 5 N (500 g on a kitchen scale under the stone). This jointing pass grinds a flat of even width along the edge, seen under a lamp as a thin unbroken line of reflected light. Four points are marked with a dot on face B, just above the bevel, 2, 6, 10 and 14 cm from the heel. A BESS edge tester (for example an Edge-On-Up PT50B) then reads each point; every point must read 500 g or more (a dull kitchen knife), or the pass is repeated. The four readings are written down as the start.
scoring: A real trial scores the measured edge; the sim, which grinds no steel, counts strokes as a stand-in, a lower bound, not a measured match: 10 strokes per face (guides give no fixed count, working a face until a burr runs heel to tip) and 10 cm of travel per point. Real edge: after the trial, without stropping, a BESS edge tester reads marked points 2, 6, 10 and 14 cm from the heel, each starting at 500 g or more; a point is sharp at 300 g or less. Put down safely: neither gripper touching the knife (a gap of 2 mm or less counts as touching), the knife flat on the block (faces within 20 degrees of level, edge within 1 cm of its top), edge within 60 degrees of facing away from the robot, so the next hand on the handle misses it; a real trial checks the top photo with a protractor. The trial scores 1.0 when most of the edge is sharpened and the knife put down safely and still for 1 s: at least 3 of the 4 points at 300 g or less; in the sim, 10 or more strokes and 12 of the 16 edge points worked on each face. It scores 0.75 when sharpened as for 1.0 but not put down safely. It scores 0.5 when 1 or 2 points read 300 g or less; in the sim, 10 or more strokes on each face but fewer than 12 points worked on a face. It scores 0.25 when no point reads 300 g or less but at least 3 read 100 g or more below their start; in the sim, 10 or more strokes on one face only, which leaves a wire edge. Otherwise it scores 0, including doing nothing. No event scores the whole trial 0. Sim stroke: the knife held (both fingers on the handle, their opening stopped by its 1.8 to 2.0 cm girth), edge below spine, its lowest point within 0.5 mm of the stone's top, moved 5 cm edge first in one pass (going back 5 mm ends a pass; edge-trailing returns count for nothing) with the blade's width 13 to 22 degrees below level, its length within 5 degrees of level, and at least 3 edge points within 1 mm of the stone. Strokes count on the face that is down. The 16 points lie about 1 cm apart, 0.5 to 16.2 cm along the 16.5 cm edge; a point is worked on a face after 10 cm of such travel. A touch with 2 cm of travel steeper than 22 degrees, or one rolling off an end (the edge 3 mm below the stone's top past an end within 0.5 s of leaving it), counts toward nothing. Where the arms end is not scored. A real trial does not score the angle. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.
reset_notes: Put the knife back flat on the block, face A down, edge away, bolster at (18.4, 0.8); the stone, holder, stand and block are fixed. For a real trial, soak the stone 10 minutes, dull the edge again with the jointing pass in the setup, and check that all four marked points read 500 g or more on the edge tester before starting.
fidelity: Nothing is ground: the sim scores strokes from the knife's pose on the stone (angle, contact, travel per edge point) as a stand-in for steel removed, and a real trial measures the edge with a BESS edge tester. No burr is felt, and the demo presses a measured median 2.4 to 3.3 N where knifemaker Bob Kramer asks 9 to 27 N; aimed harder, the drag turns the knife in the grip. The stone is dry and rigid; the knife is 140 g, with box colliders. The stand is 6 cm tall so the wrist clears the bench.
